stem: A client becomes acutely ill with high fever, diffuse erythematous rash, hypotension, confusion, and evidence of dysfunction in several organ systems. Which complication should the nurse suspect first?

options.A: Toxic shock syndrome, a toxin-mediated syndrome requiring immediate sepsis-level evaluation and treatment.
options.B: Uncomplicated allergic dermatitis because hypotension and multiorgan dysfunction are expected with a localized skin reaction.
options.C: Simple viral exanthem because rapid shock and organ dysfunction generally indicate a benign self-limited infection.
options.D: Isolated contact dermatitis because diffuse rash alone explains the systemic deterioration.

rationale: A is correct. Toxic shock syndrome is an acute toxin-mediated illness associated with toxigenic Staphylococcus aureus or streptococci and commonly presents with rapid fever, diffuse erythroderma, hypotension, and end-organ dysfunction. The syndrome can progress to sepsis and requires urgent evaluation and treatment. B, C, and D cannot adequately explain the combination of shock and multisystem involvement. CDC surveillance criteria contain specific thresholds, but those criteria are intended for public-health case classification rather than bedside diagnosis, so the item does not use them as a clinical rule.
educational_objective: Recognize the rapid combination of fever, diffuse erythroderma, hypotension, and multiorgan dysfunction as a high-risk toxic shock syndrome pattern requiring immediate escalation rather than attributing systemic shock to a benign rash illness.
source_organization: National Library of Medicine / NCBI StatPearls; Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
source_document_title: Toxic Shock Syndrome; Toxic Shock Syndrome (Other Than Streptococcal) Surveillance Case Definition
source_version_date: Current StatPearls 2026 edition accessed 2026-08-17; CDC surveillance definition page current and accessed 2026-08-17
source_locator: NCBI Toxic Shock Syndrome — Introduction/History and Physical: acute-onset toxin-mediated illness with fever, diffuse rash, hypotension and end-organ dysfunction; can progress rapidly to sepsis and organ failure. CDC TSS Case Definition — clinical manifestations include fever, diffuse macular erythroderma, hypotension and multisystem involvement; CDC explicitly notes that surveillance case definitions are for classification/counting and are not intended to make an individual clinical diagnosis.
source_claim_supported: Rapid fever, diffuse erythroderma, hypotension and multisystem organ dysfunction are characteristic of toxic shock syndrome and require urgent clinical evaluation; surveillance thresholds should not be converted into rigid bedside diagnostic rules.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing
blueprint_locator: Physiological Integrity — Physiological Adaptation: recognize signs and symptoms of shock, systemic infection and acute organ dysfunction and intervene promptly.
blueprint_topic: Physiological Adaptation — toxic shock syndrome recognition
correction_summary: Rebuilt the raw recognition item with a clinically coherent shock pattern while explicitly separating CDC surveillance criteria from bedside diagnosis. Removed unsupported universal wording and avoided numeric surveillance thresholds as clinical requirements.
audit_reviewer: OpenAI GPT-5.6 Sol — Rule 1 clinical audit + adversarial second pass

audit_findings.source_audit: Verified against current NCBI TSS review and CDC surveillance definition, including the CDC warning not to use surveillance criteria as individual clinical diagnostic rules.
audit_findings.claim_by_claim: A explains fever, diffuse rash, shock and multiorgan dysfunction. B-D cannot explain the systemic hemodynamic and organ-failure pattern.
audit_findings.choice_A: Correct; suspected TSS requires emergency escalation.
audit_findings.choice_B: Incorrect; localized allergic dermatitis does not explain this syndrome.
audit_findings.choice_C: Incorrect; a benign viral exanthem does not account for rapidly progressive shock and organ dysfunction.
audit_findings.choice_D: Incorrect; isolated dermatitis does not account for the systemic findings.
audit_findings.ambiguity_second_answer: Other causes of septic/distributive shock and rash remain possible, so the item asks what should be suspected first rather than declaring a confirmed toxin source. Only A matches the full pattern.
audit_findings.cueing: All alternatives interpret the same rash-plus-shock presentation.
audit_findings.blueprint: Recognition of shock and multiorgan deterioration fits Physiological Adaptation.
audit_findings.independent_adversarial_second_pass: Rechecked staphylococcal versus streptococcal TSS, sepsis differentials, anaphylaxis overlap, and CDC surveillance-versus-clinical use. No unsupported diagnostic threshold or second answer remained.
